note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

clarifyingQuestions: Is y a consonant?
What follows z?
Can the input contain capitals or other characters?
hints: Vowels never change, so only the 21 consonants need a rule.
The next consonant only depends on the letter, so a table of 26 entries answers every character.
Build the table once (skip vowels when stepping, wrap z to b) and join the mapped characters instead of concatenating in a loop.
invariants: the table maps each vowel to itself and each consonant to a consonant
the output has the same length as s
chooseWhen: Per-character substitution with a fixed alphabet rule
tradeoffs: A lookup table is O(1) per character; stepping through the alphabet each time is simpler but repeats work
hack2hire:69a367fe6e73e4abccc9bfe1.variantLabel: Single variant: replace each consonant by the next consonant

clarifyingQuestions: Are the columns ordered by value or by first appearance?
Do repeated values share a column?
Can the array be empty?
hints: The number of columns is the number of distinct values.
Sort the distinct values and remember the index of each one in a map.
Each row is a fresh list of zeros of that width with a 1 at the mapped index; never reuse one row object for several rows.
invariants: every row contains exactly one 1
column j corresponds to the j-th smallest distinct value
chooseWhen: Encoding categorical integers as indicator vectors
tradeoffs: A value-to-index map makes each row O(d) to build; comparing against every column is the same order but does d comparisons per row
hack2hire:68f599dba269f53ea0eff890.variantLabel: Single variant: one-hot matrix with sorted distinct columns

constraints: operands are single characters from A-Z, a-z, 0-9
clarifyingQuestions: Are operands always a single character?
Which operators can appear, and are any unary?
Should invalid input be reported?
hints: In prefix form an operator is complete once both of its operands are complete.
Operands keep their order in postfix form; only operators move, to just after their second operand.
Keep a stack of open operators with a count of finished operands; on each finished operand, pop and emit every operator whose count reaches two.
invariants: the stack holds the open operators in nesting order
each open operator has 0 or 1 finished operand
chooseWhen: Converting between expression notations in linear time
tradeoffs: The left-to-right stack avoids recursion and quadratic string building; the right-to-left string stack is shorter to write but concatenates long strings
hack2hire:67806bd26fee41e51af73dde.variantLabel: Single variant: prefix to postfix conversion

constraints: groups contain one or more letters or "." and are not nested; no "*" inside a group; "*" never follows "*" or "("
clarifyingQuestions: Must the whole text match, or is a substring match enough?
Can a group contain "."?
Can "*" follow "."?
hints: Split the pattern into units first; each unit is fixed text (letters and dots) with an optional star.
Let dp[i][u] say whether the suffix of text from i matches the units from u onward.
An unstarred unit of length g needs its contents at i and dp[i + g][u + 1]; a starred one is dp[i][u + 1] or (contents at i and dp[i + g][u]); fill i from the end.
invariants: dp[len(text)][u] is true exactly when every unit from u on is starred
a starred unit consumes whole copies of its contents only
chooseWhen: Pattern matching with Kleene star over fixed-length units
tradeoffs: The table is polynomial; backtracking is shorter but exponential on patterns like many starred units before a mismatch
hack2hire:67a23c6bc5f86173882e3d8d.variantLabel: Single variant: whole-string match with starred letters and groups

clarifyingQuestions: Are diagonal cells connected?
What is returned when there is no land?
Is the answer the sum, the size or the number of islands?
hints: Each island is a connected component of positive cells.
Flood each unvisited land cell and add the values you reach.
Use an explicit stack (not recursion) and mark cells when you push them, so a 200 x 200 snake does not overflow the call stack.
invariants: every land cell is counted in exactly one island sum
a cell is marked visited before its neighbours are explored
chooseWhen: Connected components with weights on a grid
tradeoffs: An explicit stack avoids recursion limits; union-find handles streaming cells but needs more bookkeeping

clarifyingQuestions: What exactly makes a schedule valid: distinct humans per task, distinct models per task, workload limits?
Is any valid schedule accepted, or a specific one?
What should be returned when no valid schedule exists?
hints: A task needs k different humans and k different models, so k must not exceed either count.
Choosing the least loaded human with the smallest index keeps loads within one of each other.
Prove that this choice is round robin: the q-th assignment overall goes to human q mod totalHuman and model q mod totalModel, and k consecutive values are distinct.
invariants: after q assignments, human loads differ by at most one and the first q mod totalHuman humans carry the extra one
the k assignments of a task use k consecutive indices
chooseWhen: Balanced assignment of resources to repeated jobs
tradeoffs: The closed form is O(1) per assignment; the literal greedy is easier to trust but scans every human and model

constraints: every triple has three strings of 1 to 8 characters from a-z and 0-9
clarifyingQuestions: Are labels like "t01" accepted?
May a task appear more than k times?
Are triples in the wrong order (for example a human in the model slot) invalid?
hints: Validity splits into label format, per-task counts and per-task distinctness.
Parse each label once: the right letter, then a positive decimal without leading zeros within range.
Count triples per task and keep sets of (task, human) and (task, model) pairs; a repeated pair or a count different from k makes the schedule invalid.
invariants: each (task, human) and (task, model) pair is seen at most once in a valid schedule
a valid schedule has exactly totalTask * k triples
chooseWhen: Checking a proposed assignment against per-group distinctness rules
tradeoffs: Hash sets give a linear check; comparing all pairs inside each task is simpler but quadratic in k
hack2hire:69fc131a574d87bc49005a6c.variantLabel: Variant 2 of 2: validate a proposed schedule

constraints: function names: a lowercase letter or "_" followed by up to 15 of a-z, 0-9, "_"
values nest at most 3 levels; lists and objects have at most 6 items; object keys are 1 to 8 of a-z and "_"
integers within +-1e9; strings up to 12 printable ASCII characters
clarifyingQuestions: Should true and 1, or 1 and "1", give the same key?
Does the order of keyword arguments matter?
How are unhashable arguments such as lists and dicts handled?
hints: The key must be equal exactly when the calls are equal, and stable across runs (no id() or randomised hashing).
Serialise every value with a type tag, so true, 1 and "1" differ, and write object keys in sorted order so keyword order does not matter.
Use the canonical string as the key of an insertion-ordered map: delete and re-insert on a hit, evict the first key when the map is over capacity.
invariants: two calls have equal keys exactly when they are the same call
the map iteration order is least to most recently used
chooseWhen: Memoising calls whose arguments are unhashable or order-insensitive
tradeoffs: A canonical string is easy to persist and compare; nested tuples avoid string building but cannot distinguish True from 1 in Python
hack2hire:6a2db7bc5117d1b543565e24.variantLabel: Variant 1 of 2: canonical keys for positional and keyword arguments

constraints: at most 50 functions with at most 6 parameters each
every call binds each parameter at most once and binds every required parameter
values as in variant 1 (nesting at most 3, at most 6 items, integers within +-1e9)
clarifyingQuestions: Do f(1) and f(a=1) hit the same entry?
Is an omitted argument the same as passing its default explicitly?
Can a call be invalid for its signature?
hints: Two calls are the same exactly when every parameter ends up with the same value.
Bind positional arguments by position, keywords by name and fill the rest from the defaults.
Serialise the bound values in parameter order with type tags; the parameter order fixes the layout, so the names need not be in the key.
invariants: the bound value list has one entry per parameter
two calls have equal keys exactly when their bound values are the same
chooseWhen: Memoising functions called with a mix of positional, keyword and default arguments
tradeoffs: Binding first makes equivalent spellings share one entry; keying on the raw args and kwargs is simpler but misses those hits
hack2hire:6a2db7be5117d1b543565e25.variantLabel: Variant 2 of 2: signature-normalised keys with defaults

clarifyingQuestions: Does the count include a day on which nothing changes?
Are diagonal neighbours counted?
Is the update simultaneous or in reading order?
hints: A plant can only become infected on the day after one of its neighbours was infected.
Keep a counter of infected neighbours for every healthy plant and update it only when a neighbour changes.
Process infections day by day: the plants infected on day d raise their neighbours' counters, and those reaching threshold form day d + 1.
invariants: a healthy plant's counter equals its infected neighbours at the end of the current day
each plant enters a frontier at most once
chooseWhen: Simultaneous threshold spreading on a grid
tradeoffs: Counters make the total work O(8 m n); repeated full-grid simulation is O(days * m * n)
hack2hire:69d414a179bf03c0074bcec1.variantLabel: Variant 1 of 5: number of spreading days

clarifyingQuestions: What is the energy before the elevator?
Is the answer the time or the floor k?
Can k be 0 or n?
hints: The energy before stair floor i (counting from 0) is k * e1 - i * e2, so feasibility only needs the last floor: k * e1 - (n - k - 1) * e2 > 0.
That condition is monotone in k, so binary search the smallest feasible k; k = n is always feasible.
Scan k upward: k * t1 + (n - k) is a lower bound on the total for k, which only grows faster than the stair savings once it passes the best; stop there.
invariants: every k at least the smallest feasible one is feasible
the best time never increases during the scan
chooseWhen: Choosing a switch point between two cost regimes
tradeoffs: Pruning keeps typical inputs fast; the plain double loop is the same in the worst case but never stops early
hack2hire:69ebd458068f42e15508912a.variantLabel: Single variant: best switch from elevator to stairs

clarifyingQuestions: How is equiv given: as a callable, a key function or pairs?
Are the groups ordered by first appearance and the elements by index?
Are groups contiguous subarrays or arbitrary subsets?
hints: An equivalence given by pairs is the connected components of the graph on values.
Union-find merges the pairs in near-linear time.
Walk nums once: the first time a root is seen it opens a new group; append each element to its root's group.
invariants: two values share a root exactly when they are connected by pairs
groups appear in the order of their first element
chooseWhen: Grouping items by an equivalence given through generating pairs
tradeoffs: Union-find is near linear; label propagation is simple but can take many rounds on long chains
hack2hire:68dc36c49736cfa4e9062419.variantLabel: Single variant: group elements by a generated equivalence
